taxonomy_or_method_families.name: Survey Literature
taxonomy_or_method_families.description: Comprehensive reviews covering LLM architectures, agent frameworks, and evaluation taxonomies (P1, P2, P3, P4, P5, P6, P7, P9, P10, P11).

taxonomy_or_method_families.name: Benchmark Studies
taxonomy_or_method_families.description: Specific evaluation frameworks designed to test tool use and agent capabilities (P8).

taxonomy_or_method_families.name: Commentary
taxonomy_or_method_families.description: Perspectives on evaluation gaps in specific domains like clinical settings (P12).

synthesis_groups.name: Planning and Long-term Task Capabilities
synthesis_groups.question_answered: How are planning and long-term task capabilities evaluated?
consensus: Planning is recognized as a core module in agent architecture, often integrated with memory and action modules (P4, P5, P6).
Long-term task capabilities are evaluated through simulation environments (Agent-Based Modeling) and specific benchmarks (P11, P12).
Current LLMs face limitations in long-context modeling, which hinders long-term task execution (P3).
heterogeneity: Evaluation of planning varies from internal reasoning assessment (P9) to simulation of complex workflows (P11, P12).
synthesis_groups.boundary: Focuses on architectural components and simulation-based assessment rather than raw performance metrics.

synthesis_groups.name: Tool Use Evaluation
synthesis_groups.question_answered: How is tool use evaluated, and what are the metrics?
consensus: Tool use is evaluated based on the 'Three Ws': Whether (invocation), Which (retrieval), and How (usage) (P10).
Key metrics include API call correctness, retrieval accuracy (MRR, NDCG), tool selection accuracy, and parameter name F1 score (P8, P9).
Benchmarks like API-Bank and ToolBench provide standardized environments for testing tool-augmented LLMs (P2, P8).
heterogeneity: Some evaluations focus on response quality (Rouge-L) while others focus on execution correctness (P8, P9).
synthesis_groups.boundary: Excludes multi-modal tool interaction in depth, though briefly mentioned (P10).

synthesis_groups.name: Memory and Context Management
synthesis_groups.question_answered: How is memory and context management evaluated?
consensus: Memory is categorized into short-term, long-term, and hybrid structures (P4, P5).
Evaluation focuses on the ability to retrieve relevant information and maintain context over interactions (P9).
Hallucination rates are a critical metric for assessing memory integrity (P3).
heterogeneity: Memory evaluation is often implicit within task success rates rather than a standalone metric (P3, P9).
synthesis_groups.boundary: Does not deeply cover specific memory architectures (e.g., vector databases) beyond their general utility.

synthesis_groups.name: Collaboration and Multi-agent Systems
synthesis_groups.question_answered: How are collaboration and multi-agent capabilities evaluated?
consensus: Collaboration is evaluated through sociability metrics (language proficiency, cooperation, negotiation) (P6).
Agent-based modeling and simulation (ABM) are used to evaluate social dynamics and collective behavior (P11).
Multi-agent collaboration is assessed via task completion rates and consensus answers in simulated environments (P9).
heterogeneity: Evaluation ranges from simple task cooperation (P9) to complex social simulation (P11).
synthesis_groups.boundary: Limited focus on adversarial multi-agent interactions compared to cooperative ones.

synthesis_groups.name: Evaluation Design, Metrics, Reproducibility, and Validity Risks
synthesis_groups.question_answered: What are the task designs, metrics, reproducibility, and validity risks?
consensus: Task designs range from static benchmarks (MMLU, MATH) to dynamic environments (DynaBench, API-Bank) (P1, P2, P8).
Metrics include accuracy, F1, MRR, Elo ratings, and cost/latency (P1, P2, P7, P9).
Reproducibility is adequate in benchmarks like API-Bank (code/data available) but varies in surveys (P1, P8).
Validity risks include hallucination, adversarial attacks, bias, and the subjectivity of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluations (P2, P3, P6, P9, P12).
heterogeneity: Short-term evaluations often fail to capture long-horizon performance drift (P9).
Human-crafted benchmarks may not capture emergent abilities (P2, P12).
synthesis_groups.boundary: Covers general evaluation challenges applicable across all agent capabilities.

cross_study_comparability.observation: Surveys (P1-P11) provide taxonomies and frameworks, while Benchmarks (P8) provide concrete metrics and data. Commentary (P12) critiques the gap between benchmarks and real-world application.
While accuracy is common, specific agent metrics like 'pass^k' for consistency and 'sociability' for collaboration are emerging (P2, P6, P9).
There is a shift from single-task evaluation to complex, multi-step, and long-horizon evaluations (P8, P9, P11).

evidence_gaps.description: Current benchmarks often focus on short episodes or single interactions, lacking the ability to capture performance drift or cumulative effects over time (P9).
Code-based methods are inflexible for open-ended responses, and LLM-as-a-Judge approaches introduce complexity and subjectivity (P9).
Standardized benchmarks (e.g., MedQA) are insufficient for capturing the full range of capabilities in complex domains like clinical settings (P12).
Role-based access control, reliability guarantees, and compliance requirements in enterprise environments are often overlooked (P9).

claims.claim: LLM Agents are evaluated through a combination of modular architecture analysis (Planning, Memory, Action) and task-specific benchmarks.
claims.boundary: Applies to autonomous agents designed for general-purpose task solving.

claims.claim: Tool use evaluation requires a multi-dimensional approach involving invocation accuracy, retrieval precision, and parameter correctness.
claims.boundary: Specifically applies to text-based API and tool-augmented LLMs.

claims.claim: Evaluation validity is threatened by hallucinations, adversarial attacks, and the limitations of static benchmarks in capturing emergent or long-term behaviors.
claims.boundary: Highlights risks inherent in current evaluation methodologies.

claims.claim: Reproducibility varies significantly; while some benchmarks provide open-source code and data, surveys often rely on existing literature without explicit implementation details.
claims.boundary: Based on the provided evidence cards regarding code availability.

recommended_outline.content: Overview of the shift from evaluating LLMs to evaluating agents (P2, P4, P9).
Evaluation of Planning, Memory, and Tool Use (P4, P5, P6, P8, P9, P10).
Social simulation, cooperation, and adversarial robustness (P6, P9, P11).
Taxonomies, metrics (accuracy, consistency, cost), and specific benchmarks (API-Bank, ToolBench, HELM) (P1, P2, P7, P8, P9).
Hallucination, adversarial attacks, privacy, and the 'LLM-as-a-Judge' problem (P2, P3, P6, P9, P12).
Long-horizon evaluation, enterprise-specific benchmarks, and high-fidelity simulations (P9, P12).
